claim: The Alphaproteobacteria is an extraordinarily diverse and ancient group of bacteria.
source: The Alphaproteobacteria is an extraordinarily diverse and ancient group of bacteria.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The Alphaproteobacteria encompasses the mitochondrial lineage.
source: The Alphaproteobacteria is an extraordinarily diverse and disparate group of bacteria and well-known to most biologists for also encompassing the mitochondrial lineage (Williams et al., 2007; Roger et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2007 and Roger et al., 2017.

claim: Pelagibacter ubique is one of the most abundant cells on Earth.
source: The Alphaproteobacteria has massively diversified since its origin, giving rise to, for example, some of the most abundant (e.g. Pelagibacter ubique) and metabolically versatile (e.g. Rhodobacter sphaeroides) cells on Earth (Giovannoni, 2017; Madigan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giovannoni, 2017.

claim: Rhodobacter sphaeroides is one of the most metabolically versatile cells on Earth.
source: The Alphaproteobacteria has massively diversified since its origin, giving rise to, for example, some of the most abundant (e.g. Pelagibacter ubique) and metabolically versatile (e.g. Rhodobacter sphaeroides) cells on Earth (Giovannoni, 2017; Madigan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Madigan et al., 2009.

claim: Eight major orders are well recognized in the Alphaproteobacteria: Caulobacterales, Rhizobiales, Rhodobacterales, Pelagibacterales, Sphingomonadales, Rhodospirillales, Holosporales and Rickettsiales.
source: Today, eight major orders are well recognized, namely the Caulobacterales, Rhizobiales, Rhodobacterales, Pelagibacterales, Sphingomonadales, Rhodospirillales, Holosporales and Rickettsiales (the latter two formerly grouped into the Rickettsiales sensu lato), and their interrelationships have also recently become better understood (Viklund et al., 2012; Viklund et al., 2013; Rodríguez-Ezpeleta and Embley, 2012; Wang and Wu, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The Holosporales and Rickettsiales were formerly grouped into the Rickettsiales sensu lato.
source: Today, eight major orders are well recognized, namely the Caulobacterales, Rhizobiales, Rhodobacterales, Pelagibacterales, Sphingomonadales, Rhodospirillales, Holosporales and Rickettsiales (the latter two formerly grouped into the Rickettsiales sensu lato), and their interrelationships have also recently become better understood (Viklund et al., 2012; Viklund et al., 2013; Rodríguez-Ezpeleta and Embley, 2012; Wang and Wu, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about historical taxonomic grouping.

claim: Ferla et al. (2013) grouped the eight orders into two subclasses: the subclass Rickettsiidae comprising the order Rickettsiales and Pelagibacterales, and the subclass Caulobacteridae comprising all other orders.
source: These eight orders were grouped into two subclasses by Ferla et al. (2013): the subclass Rickettsiidae comprising the order Rickettsiales and Pelagibacterales, and the subclass Caulobacteridae comprising all other orders.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferla et al., 2013.

claim: The Pelagibacterales have A + T%-rich genomes.
source: Such diversity encompasses a broad spectrum of genome (nucleotide) and proteome (amino acid) compositions (e.g. the A + T%-rich Pelagibacterales versus the G + C%-rich Acetobacteraceae) and molecular evolutionary rates (e.g. the fast-evolving Pelagibacteriales, Rickettsiales or Holosporales versus many slow-evolving species in the Rhodospirillales) (Ettema and Andersson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ettema and Andersson, 2009.

claim: The Acetobacteraceae have G + C%-rich genomes.
source: Such diversity encompasses a broad spectrum of genome (nucleotide) and proteome (amino acid) compositions (e.g. the A + T%-rich Pelagibacterales versus the G + C%-rich Acetobacteraceae) and molecular evolutionary rates (e.g. the fast-evolving Pelagibacteriales, Rickettsiales or Holosporales versus many slow-evolving species in the Rhodospirillales) (Ettema and Andersson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ettema and Andersson, 2009.

claim: The Pelagibacteriales, Rickettsiales and Holosporales are fast-evolving.
source: Such diversity encompasses a broad spectrum of genome (nucleotide) and proteome (amino acid) compositions (e.g. the A + T%-rich Pelagibacterales versus the G + C%-rich Acetobacteraceae) and molecular evolutionary rates (e.g. the fast-evolving Pelagibacteriales, Rickettsiales or Holosporales versus many slow-evolving species in the Rhodospirillales) (Ettema and Andersson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ettema and Andersson, 2009.

claim: Many species in the Rhodospirillales are slow-evolving.
source: Such diversity encompasses a broad spectrum of genome (nucleotide) and proteome (amino acid) compositions (e.g. the A + T%-rich Pelagibacterales versus the G + C%-rich Acetobacteraceae) and molecular evolutionary rates (e.g. the fast-evolving Pelagibacteriales, Rickettsiales or Holosporales versus many slow-evolving species in the Rhodospirillales) (Ettema and Andersson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ettema and Andersson, 2009.

claim: Long-branch attraction occurs between the Rickettsiales and Pelagibacterales, especially when including mitochondria.
source: This diversity may lead to pervasive artefacts when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria, for example, long-branch attraction (LBA) between the Rickettsiales and Pelagibacterales, especially when including mitochondria (Rodríguez-Ezpeleta and Embley, 2012; Viklund et al., 2012; Viklund et al., 2013; Luo, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies that identified this phylogenetic artifact.

claim: The genome of 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata' is 1,792,168 bp in size.
source: Genome size	1,792,168 bp
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing genome features.

claim: The genome of 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata' has an A + T% content of 56.58%.
source: A + T% content	56.58%
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing genome features.

claim: 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata' belongs to the 'Candidatus Paracaedibacteraeae' family.
source: Family	'Candidatus Paracaedibacteraeae'
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing taxonomic classification.

claim: 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata' belongs to the Holosporales order.
source: Order	Holosporales
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing taxonomic classification.

claim: The Stachyamoeba-associated rickettsialean belongs to the Rickettsiales order.
source: Order	Rickettsiales
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing taxonomic classification.

claim: The Peranema-associated rickettsialean belongs to the Rickettsiales order.
source: Order	Rickettsiales
evidence: Data from Table 1 showing taxonomic classification.

claim: The three novel genomes are small with a reduced gene number and high A + T% content, strongly suggesting an endosymbiotic lifestyle.
source: The three genomes are small with a reduced gene number and high A + T% content, strongly suggesting an endosymbiotic lifestyle (Table 1).
evidence: Inference based on genome characteristics shown in Table 1.

claim: The closest 16S rRNA gene to that of the Stachyamoeba-associated rickettsialean belongs to Rickettsia massiliae str. AZT80, with only 88% identity.
source: As of February 2018, the closest 16S rRNA gene to that of the Stachyamoeba-associated rickettsialean belongs to Rickettsia massiliae str. AZT80, with only 88% identity.
evidence: Data from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The closest 16S rRNA gene to that of the Peranema-associated rickettsialean belongs to an endosymbiont of Acanthamoeba sp. UWC8, which is only 92% identical.
source: On the other hand, the closest 16S rRNA gene to that of the Peranema-associated rickettsialean belongs to an endosymbiont of Acanthamoeba sp. UWC8, which is only 92% identical.
evidence: Data from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (together with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59) and Holosporales have divergent proteome amino acid compositions compared to other alphaproteobacteria.
source: The average-linkage clustering of amino acid compositions shows that the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (together with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59) and Holosporales are clearly distinct from other alphaproteobacteria. This indicates that these three taxa have divergent proteome amino acid compositions (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales have the lowest GARP:FIMNKY amino acid ratios in all the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: These taxa also have the lowest GARP:FIMNKY amino acid ratios in all the Alphaproteobacteria (Figure 1A; GARP amino acids are encoded by G + C%-rich codons, whereas FIMNKY amino acids are encoded by A + T%-rich codons. Proteomes that have low GARP:FIMNKY ratios are compositionally biased and therefore come from A + T%-rich genomes); the Pelagibacterales (including alphaproteobacterium HIMB59) being the most divergent, followed by the Rickettsiales and then the Holosporales.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GARP amino acids are encoded by G + C%-rich codons.
source: GARP amino acids are encoded by G + C%-rich codons, whereas FIMNKY amino acids are encoded by A + T%-rich codons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about codon usage.

claim: FIMNKY amino acids are encoded by A + T%-rich codons.
source: GARP amino acids are encoded by G + C%-rich codons, whereas FIMNKY amino acids are encoded by A + T%-rich codons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about codon usage.

claim: Proteomes that have low GARP:FIMNKY ratios are compositionally biased and come from A + T%-rich genomes.
source: Proteomes that have low GARP:FIMNKY ratios are compositionally biased and therefore come from A + T%-rich genomes
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between codon usage and genome composition.

claim: There is a strong correlation between genome G + C% and proteome GARP:FIMNKY ratios for the 120 taxa in the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: A scatter plot of genome G + C% and proteome GARP:FIMNKY ratios shows a similar clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (including alphaproteobacterium HIMB59) and Holosporales (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by the scatterplot shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Under the LG+PMSF(ES60)+F+R6 model, the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 at its base) and Holosporales form a fully supported clade.
source: As a first step to discriminate between these two alternatives, we used maximum likelihood to estimate a tree on a dataset that comprised 200 single-copy and rarely laterally transferred marker genes for the Alphaproteobacteria (as determined by Phyla-AMPHORA; see Materials and methods for more details; Wang and Wu, 2013) under the site-heterogenous model LG+PMSF(ES60)+F+R6. The resulting tree united the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales (with alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 at its base) and Holosporales in a fully supported clade (Figure 2A; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for labeled trees).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales is suggestive of a phylogenetic artefact.
source: The clustering of these three groups is suggestive of a phylogenetic artefact (e.g. long-branch attraction or LBA); indeed, such a pattern resembles the one seen in the tree of proteome amino acid compositions (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity to compositional clustering and known phylogenetic artifacts.

claim: When 50% of the most compositionally biased sites are removed, the clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales is disrupted.
source: When removing the 50% most compositionally biased (heterogeneous) sites according to ɀ (a novel metric that measures amino acid compositional disparity at a site; see Materials and methods), the clustering between the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales is disrupted (Figure 2B; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After removing compositionally biased sites, the Pelagibacterales becomes sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
source: The new more derived placements for the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales are well supported (further described below), and support tends to increase as compositionally biased sites are removed (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary data.

claim: After removing compositionally biased sites, the Holosporales becomes sister to the Rhodospirillales.
source: When compositional heterogeneity is further decreased by removing 50% of the most compositionally biased sites, the Holosporales becomes sister to the Rhodospirillales (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2A; and see also Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales and Holosporales.
source: On the other hand, removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of these three long-branched groups (Supplementary file 2B), suggesting that high evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis results in Supplementary file 2B.

claim: High evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: On the other hand, removing fast-evolving sites does not disrupt the clustering of these three long-branched groups (Supplementary file 2B), suggesting that high evolutionary rates per site are not a major confounding factor when inferring the phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that removing fast-evolving sites does not change the topology.

claim: The Holosporales has traditionally been considered part of the Rickettsiales sensu lato because it appears as sister to the Rickettsiales in many trees.
source: The Holosporales has traditionally been considered part of the Rickettsiales sensu lato because it appears as sister to the Rickettsiales in many trees (e.g. Hess et al., 2016; Montagna et al., 2013; Santos and Massard, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Holosporales is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes.
source: It is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes, and such a lifestyle is shared with all other members of the Rickettsiales (with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean; see Castelli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the lifestyle of Holosporales members, with a citation noting an exception.

claim: All members of the Rickettsiales share an endosymbiotic lifestyle, with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean.
source: It is exclusively composed of endosymbiotic bacteria living within diverse eukaryotes, and such a lifestyle is shared with all other members of the Rickettsiales (with the possible exception of a recently reported ectosymbiotic rickettialean; see Castelli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castelli et al., 2018.

claim: When compositional heterogeneity is decreased and the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, and alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 are removed, the Holosporales moves to a derived position well within the Rhodospirillales.
source: Similarly, when the long-branched and compositionally biased Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, and alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 (plus the extremely long-branched genera Holospora and 'Candidatus Hepatobacter') are removed, after compositional heterogeneity had been decreased through site removal, the Holosporales move to a much more derived position well within the Rhodospirillales (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: The Holosporales branches as sister to a subgroup of rhodospirillaleans that includes Micavibrio aeruginosavorus and Rhodocista centenaria (the Azospirillaceae).
source: Specifically, the Holosporales now consistently branches as sister to a subgroup of rhodospirillaleans that includes, among others, the epibiotic predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus and the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodocista centenaria (the Azospirillaceae, see below) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The placement of the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae has nearly full support under both maximum likelihood (>95% UFBoot) and Bayesian inference (>0.95 posterior probability).
source: This new placement of the Holosporales has nearly full support under both maximum likelihood (>95% UFBoot; see Figure 3) and Bayesian inference (>0.95 posterior probability; see Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by statistical support values from phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Three different analyses independently converge to support a derived origin of the Holosporales within the Rhodospirillales: removal of compositionally biased sites, data recoding into four-character states, and data recoding into six-character states.
source: Thus, three different analyses independently converge to the same pattern and support a derived origin of the Holosporales within the Rhodospirillales: (1) removal of compositionally biased sites (Figure 3A), (2) data recoding into four-character states using the dataset-specific scheme S4 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 7), and (3) data recoding into six-character states using the dataset-specific scheme S6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8); each of these strategies had to be combined with the removal of the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59, and Rickettsiales to recover this phylogenetic position for the Holosporales.
evidence: Supported by multiple independent phylogenetic analyses shown in figures.

claim: Bayesian inference using the CAT-Poisson+Γ4 model on a dataset with 50% of compositionally biased sites removed recovered the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae.
source: A fourth independent analysis further supports a derived placement of the Holosporales nested within the Rhodospirillales. Bayesian inference using the CAT-Poisson+Γ4 model, on a dataset whose compositional heterogeneity had been decreased by removing 50% of the most compositionally biased sites but for which no taxon had been removed, also recovered the Holosporales as sister to the Azospirillaceae (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Rhodospirillales comprises five well-supported families.
source: Such broad sampling reveals trees with five clear subgroups within the Rhodospirillales that are well-supported in most of our analyses (e.g. Figures 2B and 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The Acetobacteraceae comprises acetic acid, acidophilic, and photosynthetic bacteria.
source: First is the Acetobacteraceae which comprises acetic acid (e.g. Acetobacter oboediens), acidophilic (e.g. Acidisphaera rubrifaciens), and photosynthetic (bacteriochlorophyll-containing; for example, Rubritepida flocculans) bacteria.
evidence: This is a description of the diversity within the Acetobacteraceae family.

claim: The Acetobacteraceae is strongly supported and relatively divergent from all other families within the Rhodospirillales.
source: The Acetobacteraceae is strongly supported and relatively divergent from all other families within the Rhodospirillales.
evidence: This is a statement about phylogenetic support and divergence.

claim: The Rhodospirillaceae includes the type species Rhodospirillum rubrum and magnetotactic bacterial genera Magnetospirillum, Magnetovibrio and Magnetospira.
source: Sister to the Acetobacteraceae is another subgroup that comprises many photosynthetic bacteria, including the type species for the Rhodospirillales, Rhodospirillum rubrum, as well as the magnetotactic bacterial genera Magnetospirillum, Magnetovibrio and Magnetospira (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Rhodospirillaceae family.

claim: The Holosporales is sister to the Azospirillaceae within the Rhodospirillales.
source: As described above, when artefacts are accounted for, the Holosporales most likely branches within the Rhodospirillales and therefore we suggest the Holosporales sensu Szokoli et al. (2016) be lowered in rank to the family Holosporaceae (containing for example, Caedibacter sp. 37–49 and 'Candidatus Paracaedibacter symbiosus'), which is sister to the Azospirillaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus.
source: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic (neither periplasmic nor intracellular) predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus, among others.
evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Azospirillaceae family.

claim: Micavibrio aeruginosavorus is an epibiotic predator that is neither periplasmic nor intracellular.
source: The Azospirillaceae contains the purple bacterium Rhodocista centenaria and the epibiotic (neither periplasmic nor intracellular) predator Micavibrio aeruginosavorus, among others.
evidence: This is a description of the lifestyle of Micavibrio aeruginosavorus.

claim: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae.
source: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3), a well-supported group that comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Rhodovibriaceae comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
source: The Holosporaceae and the Azospirillaceae clades appear to be sister to the Rhodovibriaceae fam. nov. (Figure 3), a well-supported group that comprises the purple nonsulfur bacterium Rhodovibrio salinarum, the aerobic heterotroph Kiloniella laminariae, and the marine bacterioplankter 'Candidatus Puniceispirillum marinum' (or the SAR116 clade).
evidence: This is a description of the composition of the Rhodovibriaceae family.

claim: The Geminicoccaceae is a recently proposed family within the Rhodospirillales.
source: The Geminicocacceae is a recently proposed family within the Rhodospirillales (Proença et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Proença et al., 2018.

claim: The Geminicoccaceae is currently represented by two genera, Geminicoccus and Arboriscoccus.
source: It is currently represented by only two genera, Geminicoccus and Arboriscoccus (Foesel et al., 2007; Proença et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Foesel et al., 2007 and Proença et al., 2018.

claim: Tistrella mobilis is often sister to Geminicoccus roseus with full statistical support.
source: In most of our trees, however, Tistrella mobilis is often sister to Geminicoccus roseus with full statistical support (e.g., Figures 2B and 3A, but see Figure 3—figure supplement 6 for an exception) and we therefore consider it to be part of the Geminococcaceae.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claim: The Geminicoccaceae tends to have two alternative stable positions in the analyses: either as sister to all other families of the Rhodospirillales, or as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae.
source: Interestingly, the Geminicoccaceae tends to have two alternative stable positions in our analyses, either as sister to all other families of the Rhodospirillales (e.g. Figures 2A and 3A), or as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae (i.e. representing the most basal lineage of free-living alphaproteobacteria; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 6, or Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claim: Analyses designed to alleviate compositional heterogeneity favor the placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to all other orders of the Caulobacteridae.
source: Our analyses designed to alleviate compositional heterogeneity, specifically site removal and recoding (without taxon removal), favor the latter position for the Geminicoccaceae (Figures 2B and 3B).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3B.

claim: As compositionally biased sites are progressively removed, support for the affiliation of the Geminicoccaceae with the Rhodospirillales decreases.
source: Moreover, as compositionally biased sites are progressively removed, support for the affiliation of the Geminicoccaceae with the Rhodospirillales decreases, and after 50% of the sites have been removed, the Geminicoccaceae emerges as sister to all other free-living alphaproteobacteria with strong support (>95% UFBoot; Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with progressive site removal shown in Supplementary file 2A.

claim: The LG4X model places the Geminicoccaceae in a derived position as sister to the Acetobacteraceae.
source: In further agreement with this trend, the much simpler model LG4X places the Geminicocacceae in a derived position as sister to the Acetobacteraceae (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), but as model complexity increases, and compositional heterogeneity is reduced, the Geminicoccaceae moves closer to the base of the Alphaproteobacteria (Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The Geminicoccaceae may be a novel and independent order-level lineage in the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: Such a placement suggests that the Geminicoccaceae may be a novel and independent order-level lineage in the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic placement.

claim: The removal of compositionally biased sites (from 30% on) supports a derived placement of the Pelagibacterales as sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
source: The removal of compositionally biased sites (from 30% on; 16,320 out of 54,400 sites; see Supplementary file 2A, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), data recoding into four-character states (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), and a set of the most compositionally homogeneous genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D), all support a derived placement of the Pelagibacterales as sister to the Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claim: The Caulobacterales is sister to the Rhizobiales, and the Rhodobacterales is sister to both.
source: The Caulobacterales is sister to the Rhizobiales, and the Rhodobacterales sister to both (e.g. Figures 2B and 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The interrelationships among Caulobacterales, Rhizobiales, and Rhodobacterales become very robustly supported as compositional heterogeneity is increasingly alleviated.
source: This is consistent throughout most of our results and such interrelationships become very robustly supported as compositional heterogeneity is increasingly alleviated (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with progressive site removal shown in Supplementary file 2A.

claim: The placement of the Rickettsiales as sister to the Caulobacteridae remains stable across different analyses.
source: The placement of the Rickettsiales as sister to the Caulobacteridae (i.e. all other alphaproteobacteria) remains stable across different analyses (see Supplementary file 2A, and also Figure 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2); this is also true when the other long-branched taxa, the Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales, and even the Beta- Gammaproteobacteria outgroup, are removed (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures and supplementary files.

claim: The interrelationships inside the Rickettsiales order remain uncertain.
source: Yet, the interrelationships inside the Rickettsiales order remain uncertain; the 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae' becomes sister to the Anaplasmataceae when fast-evolving sites are removed (Supplementary file 2B), but to the Rickettsiaceae when compositionally biased sites are removed (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses with different site removal strategies shown in supplementary files.

claim: The placement of alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is uncertain.
source: The placement of alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is uncertain (e.g. see Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5; in contrast to Grote et al., 2012); taxon-removal analyses suggest that alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is sister to the Caulobacteridae (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), but the inclusion of any other long-branched group immediately destabilizes this position (e.g. see Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in multiple figures.

claim: Alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is not closely related to the Pelagibacterales.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that suggest that alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 is not closely related to the Pelagibacterales (Viklund et al., 2013; Martijn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Viklund et al., 2013 and Martijn et al., 2018.

claim: The Rickettsiales sensu lato (i.e. the Rickettsiales and Holosporales) is polyphyletic.
source: A combination of these strategies reveals that the Rickettsiales sensu lato (i.e. the Rickettsiales and Holosporales) is polyphyletic.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic analyses presented.

claim: The Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales.
source: Our analyses suggest that the Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales, and that therefore this taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family (see Figures 2B and 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The Holosporales taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family.
source: Our analyses suggest that the Holosporales is derived within the Rhodospirillales, and that therefore this taxon should be lowered in rank and renamed the Holosporaceae family (see Figures 2B and 3).
evidence: This is a taxonomic proposal based on phylogenetic results.

claim: The Rhodospirillales might be a paraphyletic order.
source: The same methods suggest that the Rhodospirillales might indeed be a paraphyletic order and that the Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae (e.g. Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae.
source: The same methods suggest that the Rhodospirillales might indeed be a paraphyletic order and that the Geminicoccaceae could be a separate lineage that is sister to the Caulobacteridae (e.g. Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a speculation based on phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The diversity of the Rhodospirillales can be grouped into at least five well-supported major families.
source: These two results, combined with our broader sampling, reorganize the internal phylogenetic structure of the Rhodospirillales and show that its diversity can be grouped into at least five well-supported major families (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The apparent diversity of the Holosporales has quickly increased in recent years as more intracellular bacteria living within protists have been described.
source: The apparent diversity of this group has quickly increased in recent years as more and more intracellular bacteria living within protists have been described (e.g. Hess et al., 2016; Szokoli et al., 2016; Eschbach et al., 2009; Boscaro et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies describing new members.

claim: Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015) provided apparent strong support for the monophyly of the Rickettsiales and the Holosporales based on multi-gene trees.
source: Apparent strong support for the monophyly of the Rickettsiales and the Holosporales recently came from some multi-gene trees by Wang and Wu (2014), and Wang and Wu (2015) who expanded sampling for the Holosporales.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015).

claim: An alternative placement for the Holosporales as sister to the Caulobacteridae has been reported by multiple studies.
source: However, an alternative placement for the Holosporales as sister to the Caulobacteridae has been reported by Ferla et al. (2013) based on rRNA genes, by Georgiades et al. (2011) based on 65 genes, by Schulz et al., (2015) based on 139 genes, as well as by Wang and Wu (2015) based on 26, 29, or 200 genes (see the supplementary information in Wang and Wu, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Szokoli et al. (2016) formally established the order Holosporales.
source: This placement was acknowledged by Szokoli et al. (2016), who formally established the order Holosporales.
evidence: Supported by citation to Szokoli et al. (2016).

claim: Martijn et al. (2018) recovered a number of placements for the Holosporales within the Alphaproteobacteria, but these different placements were poorly supported.
source: Most recently, Martijn et al. (2018), who used strategies to reduce compositional heterogeneity, and similarly to Wang and Wu (2015), recovered a number of placements for the Holosporales within the Alphaproteobacteria; however, these different placements for the Holosporales were poorly supported.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martijn et al. (2018).

claim: This study provides strong evidence for the hypothesis that the Holosporales is not related to the Rickettsiales.
source: Here, we provide strong evidence for the hypothesis that the Holosporales is not related to the Rickettsiales, as suggested earlier (Georgiades et al., 2011; Ferla et al., 2013; Szokoli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic analyses presented, with citations to earlier studies that suggested this hypothesis.

claim: The Holosporales is artefactually attracted to the Rickettsiales.
source: We show that the Holosporales is artefactually attracted to the Rickettsiales (e.g. Figure 2A), but as compositional bias is increasingly alleviated (through site removal and recoding), they move further away from them (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The Holosporales is placed within the Rhodopirillales as sister to the family Azospirillaceae.
source: The Holosporales is placed within the Rhodopirillales as sister to the family Azospirillaceae (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The similar lifestyles of the Holosporales and Rickettsiales are likely the outcome of convergent evolution.
source: The similar lifestyles of the Holosporales and Rickettsiales, as well as other features like the presence of an ATP/ADP translocase (Wang and Wu, 2014), are therefore likely the outcome of convergent evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic separation of the two groups.

claim: Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015) proposed that mitochondria are phylogenetically embedded within the Rickettsiales sensu lato.
source: Wang and Wu (2014), and Wang and Wu (2015) proposed that mitochondria are phylogenetically embedded within the Rickettsiales sensu lato.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang and Wu (2014) and Wang and Wu (2015).

claim: In the trees of Wang and Wu (2014, 2015), mitochondria were sister to a clade formed by the Rickettsiaceae, Anaplasmataceae and 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae', and the Holosporales was itself sister to all of them.
source: In their trees, mitochondria were sister to a clade formed by the Rickettsiaceae, Anaplasmataceae and 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae', and the Holosporales was itself sister to all of them.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic placement in the trees of Wang and Wu (2014, 2015).

claim: Wang and Wu (2014) suggested that the ancestor of mitochondria was an intracellular parasite based on the phylogenetic placement of mitochondria.
source: This phylogenetic placement for mitochondria suggested that the ancestor of mitochondria was an intracellular parasite (Wang and Wu, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Wu (2014).

claim: If the Holosporales is a derived group of rhodospirillaleans, then the argument that mitochondria necessarily evolved from parasitic alphaproteobacteria no longer holds.
source: But if the Holosporales is a derived group of rhodospirillaleans as we show here (see Figure 3), then the argument that mitochondria necessarily evolved from parasitic alphaproteobacteria no longer holds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic results presented.

claim: The sisterhood of mitochondria and the Rickettsiales sensu stricto does not imply that the two groups shared a parasitic common ancestor.
source: While the sisterhood of mitochondria and the Rickettsiales sensu stricto is still a possibility, such a relationship does not imply that the two groups shared a parasitic common ancestor (i.e. a parasitic ancestry for mitochondria).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic results.

claim: Martijn et al. (2018) suggest that mitochondria are sister to all known alphaproteobacteria, suggesting their non-parasitic ancestry.
source: The most recent analyses of Martijn et al. (2018) suggest that mitochondria are sister to all known alphaproteobacteria, also suggesting their non-parasitic ancestry.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martijn et al. (2018).

claim: Mitochondria most likely evolved from ancestral free-living alphaproteobacteria.
source: Our study, and that of Martijn et al., thus complement each other and support the view that mitochondria most likely evolved from ancestral free-living alphaproteobacteria (contra Sassera et al., 2011; Wang and Wu, 2014; Wang and Wu, 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phylogenetic results of this study and Martijn et al. (2018), with citations to contrasting views.

claim: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae.
source: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae and has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic position and historical taxonomy of the Rhodospirillales.

claim: The Rhodospirillales has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
source: The Rhodospirillales is sister to all other orders in the Caulobacteridae and has historically been subdivided into two families: the Rhodospirillaceae and the Acetobacteraceae.
evidence: This is a statement about historical taxonomy.

claim: A new family, the Geminicoccaceae, was recently established for the Rhodospirillales.
source: Recently, a new family, the Geminicoccaceae, was established for the Rhodospirillales (Proença et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Proença et al. (2018).

claim: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available.
source: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available; if it were to be confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research and a conditional taxonomic proposal.

claim: If the placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae is confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.
source: The placement of the Geminicoccaceae as sister to the Caulobacteridae needs to be further tested once more sequenced diversity for this group becomes available; if it were to be confirmed, the Geminicoccaceae should be elevated to the order level.
evidence: This is a conditional taxonomic proposal.

claim: The Acetobacteraceae is phylogenetically well-defined.
source: Whereas the Acetobacteraceae is phylogenetically well-defined, there has been considerable uncertainty about the Rhodospirillaceae (e.g. Ferla et al., 2013), primarily because of poor sampling and a lack of resolution provided by the 16S rRNA gene.
evidence: This is a statement about the phylogenetic clarity of the Acetobacteraceae.

claim: There has been considerable uncertainty about the Rhodospirillaceae, primarily because of poor sampling and a lack of resolution provided by the 16S rRNA gene.
source: Whereas the Acetobacteraceae is phylogenetically well-defined, there has been considerable uncertainty about the Rhodospirillaceae (e.g. Ferla et al., 2013), primarily because of poor sampling and a lack of resolution provided by the 16S rRNA gene.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferla et al. (2013).

claim: This study subdivides the Rhodospirillaceae sensu lato into three subgroups.
source: We subdivide the Rhodospirillaceae sensu lato into three subgroups (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Rhodospirillaceae sensu stricto is restricted to the subgroup that is sister to the Acetobacteracae.
source: We restrict the Rhodospirillaceae sensu stricto to the subgroup that is sister to the Acetobacteracae (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a taxonomic proposal based on phylogenetic results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The other two subgroups within the Rhodospirillaceae sensu lato are the Rhodovibriaceae and the Azospirillaceae.
source: The other two subgroups are the Rhodovibriaceae and the Azospirillaceae; the latter is sister to the Holosporaceae (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Azospirillaceae is sister to the Holosporaceae.
source: The other two subgroups are the Rhodovibriaceae and the Azospirillaceae; the latter is sister to the Holosporaceae (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: This study has updated the higher-level taxonomy of the Alphaproteobacteria based on fairly robust phylogenetic patterns.
source: Based on our fairly robust phylogenetic patterns, we have updated the higher-level taxonomy of the Alphaproteobacteria (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the taxonomic contributions of the study.

claim: The Magnetococcales is excluded from the Alphaproteobacteria class because of its divergent nature.
source: We exclude the Magnetococcales from the Alphaproteobacteria class because of its divergent nature (e.g. see Figure 1 in Esser et al., 2007 which shows that many of Magnetococcus' genes are more similar to those of beta-, and gammaproteobacteria).
evidence: Supported by citation to Esser et al., 2007.

claim: This study endorses the Magnetococcia class as proposed by Parks et al. (2018).
source: In agreement with its intermediate phylogenetic placement, we endorse the Magnetococcia class as proposed by Parks et al. (2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parks et al. (2018).

claim: The Alphaproteobacteria class comprises two subclasses: the Rickettsidae and the Caulobacteridae.
source: At the highest level we define the Alphaproteobacteria class as comprising two subclasses sensu Ferla et al. (2013), the Rickettsidae and the Caulobacteridae.
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition based on phylogenetic results, with reference to Ferla et al. (2013).

claim: The Rickettsidae subclass contains the Rickettsiales.
source: The former contains the Rickettsiales, and the latter contains all other orders, which are primarily and ancestrally free-living alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition.

claim: The Caulobacteridae subclass contains all other orders, which are primarily and ancestrally free-living alphaproteobacteria.
source: The former contains the Rickettsiales, and the latter contains all other orders, which are primarily and ancestrally free-living alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition with an inference about ancestral lifestyle.

claim: The order Rickettsiales comprises three families: the Rickettsiaceae, the Anaplasmataceae, and the 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae'.
source: The order Rickettsiales comprises three families as previously defined, the Rickettsiaceae, the Anaplasmataceae, and the 'Candidatus Midichloriaceae'.
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition.

claim: The Caulobacteridae is composed of seven phylogenetically well-supported orders: the Rhodospirillales, Sneathiellales, Sphingomonadales, Pelagibacterales, Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
source: On the other hand, the Caulobacteridae is composed of seven phylogenetically well-supported orders: the Rhodospirillales, Sneathiellales, Sphingomonadales, Pelagibacterales, Rhodobacterales, Caulobacterales and Rhizobiales.
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition based on phylogenetic results.

claim: Among the many species claimed to represent new order-level lineages on the basis of 16S rRNA gene trees, only Sneathiella deserves order-level status.
source: Among the many species claimed to represent new order-level lineages on the basis of 16S rRNA gene trees (Cho and Giovannoni, 2003; Kwon et al., 2005; Kurahashi et al., 2008; Wiese et al., 2009; Harbison et al., 2017), only Sneathiella deserves order-level status (Kurahashi et al., 2008), since all others have derived placements in our trees and those published by others (Williams et al., 2012; Bazylinski et al., 2013; Venkata Ramana et al., 2013; Harbison et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The Rhodospirillales order comprises six families, three of which are new: the Holosporaceae, Azospirillaceae and Rhodovibriaceae.
source: The Rhodospirillales order comprises six families, three of which are new, namely the Holosporaceae, Azospirillaceae and Rhodovibriaceae (Table 2).
evidence: This is a taxonomic definition based on phylogenetic results.

claim: This new higher-level classification of the Alphaproteobacteria updates and expands those presented by Ferla et al. (2013), the 'Bergey's Manual of Systematics of Archaea and Bacteria', and 'The Prokaryotes'.
source: This new higher-level classification of the Alphaproteobacteria updates and expands those presented by Ferla et al. (2013), the 'Bergey's Manual of Systematics of Archaea and Bacteria' (Garrity et al., 2005; Whitman, 2015), and 'The Prokaryotes' (Rosenberg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous taxonomic works.

claim: The classification scheme proposed here could be partly harmonized with that recently proposed by Parks et al. (2018) by elevating the six families within the Rhodospirllales to the order level.
source: The classification scheme proposed here could be partly harmonized with that recently proposed by Parks et al. (2018) by elevating the six families within the Rhodospirllales to the order level; the trees by Parks et al. (2018), however, are in conflict with those shown here and many of their proposed taxa are as well.
evidence: This is a discussion of how the proposed taxonomy relates to that of Parks et al. (2018), with a note of conflict.

claim: The trees by Parks et al. (2018) are in conflict with those shown in this study.
source: The classification scheme proposed here could be partly harmonized with that recently proposed by Parks et al. (2018) by elevating the six families within the Rhodospirllales to the order level; the trees by Parks et al. (2018), however, are in conflict with those shown here and many of their proposed taxa are as well.
evidence: This is a statement about conflict between phylogenetic results.

claim: A robust phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria is a precondition for placing the mitochondrial lineage.
source: A robust phylogeny of the Alphaproteobacteria is a precondition for placing the mitochondrial lineage.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the phylogenetic framework.

claim: Including mitochondria exacerbates the already strong biases in the data and represents additional sources of artefacts in phylogenetic inference.
source: This is because including mitochondria certainly exacerbates the already strong biases in the data, and therefore represents additional sources of artefacts in phylogenetic inference (as seen in Wang and Wu, 2015) where the Holosporales is attracted by both mitochondria and the Rickettsiales).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Wu (2015) as an example.

claim: The robust phylogenetic framework developed in this study will serve as a reference for future studies that aim to place mitochondria and novel not-yet-cultured environmental diversity within the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: The robust phylogenetic framework developed here will serve as a reference for future studies that aim to place mitochondria and novel not-yet-cultured environmental diversity within the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the study's results for future research.

claim: Cultures of Viridiraptor invadens strain Virl02 were grown on the filamentous green alga Zygnema pseudogedeanum strain CCAC 0199.
source: Cultures of Viridiraptor invadens strain Virl02, the host of 'Candidatus Finniella inopinata', were grown on the filamentous green alga Zygnema pseudogedeanum strain CCAC 0199 as described in Hess and Melkonian (2013).
evidence: This is a description of the culture method, with citation to Hess and Melkonian (2013).

claim: A dataset of 200 single-copy and conserved genes was used for phylogenetic analysis.
source: A set of 200 gene markers (54,400 sites; 9.03% missing data, see Figure 2—figure supplement 6) defined by Phyla-AMPHORA was used (Wang and Wu, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used, with citation to Wang and Wu (2013).

claim: The 200 genes are single-copy and predominantly vertically inherited as assessed by congruence among them.
source: The genes are single-copy and predominantly vertically inherited as assessed by congruence among them (Wang and Wu, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Wu (2013).

claim: A novel metric ɀ was developed to measure amino acid compositional disparity at a site.
source: When removing the 50% most compositionally biased (heterogeneous) sites according to ɀ (a novel metric that measures amino acid compositional disparity at a site; see Materials and methods), the clustering between the Rickettsiales, Pelagibacterales, alphaproteobacterium HIMB59 and Holosporales is disrupted (Figure 2B; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a description of a methodological innovation.

claim: Dataset-specific profile mixture models were employed to reduce compositional artefacts.
source: Such strategies include using novel dataset-specific profile mixture models and recoding schemes, and removing sites, genes and taxa that are compositionally biased.
evidence: This is a description of methodological strategies used.

claim: Recoding schemes were employed to reduce compositional artefacts.
source: Such strategies include using novel dataset-specific profile mixture models and recoding schemes, and removing sites, genes and taxa that are compositionally biased.
evidence: This is a description of methodological strategies used.

claim: Sites, genes and taxa that are compositionally biased were removed to reduce compositional artefacts.
source: Such strategies include using novel dataset-specific profile mixture models and recoding schemes, and removing sites, genes and taxa that are compositionally biased.
evidence: This is a description of methodological strategies used.

claim: The Rickettsiales and Holosporales are not sisters to each other.
source: We show that the Rickettsiales and Holosporales (both groups of intracellular parasites of eukaryotes) are not sisters to each other, but instead, the Holosporales has a derived position within the Rhodospirillales.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The Holosporales has a derived position within the Rhodospirillales.
source: We show that the Rickettsiales and Holosporales (both groups of intracellular parasites of eukaryotes) are not sisters to each other, but instead, the Holosporales has a derived position within the Rhodospirillales.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on phylogenetic analyses.

claim: The Rickettsiales and Holosporales are both groups of intracellular parasites of eukaryotes.
source: We show that the Rickettsiales and Holosporales (both groups of intracellular parasites of eukaryotes) are not sisters to each other, but instead, the Holosporales has a derived position within the Rhodospirillales.
evidence: This is a statement about the lifestyle of these groups.

claim: This study presents an updated proposal for the higher-level taxonomy of the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: A synthesis of our results also leads to an updated proposal for the higher-level taxonomy of the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the contributions of the study.

claim: The robust consensus phylogeny will serve as a framework for future studies that aim to place mitochondria and novel environmental diversity within the Alphaproteobacteria.
source: Our robust consensus phylogeny will serve as a framework for future studies that aim to place mitochondria, and novel environmental diversity, within the Alphaproteobacteria.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the study's results for future research.
